pos: n. (the monastery and school on the Shannon founded by Ciarán in 544, the chief seat of Irish learning and annal-keeping)
etymology: Irish Cluain Mhic Nóis, the meadow of the sons of Nós, from cluain, a water meadow.
biblical_def: Clonmacnoise stands on a low ridge above the Shannon in Offaly, where the river crossing met the great east-west road across the bogs, and for six hundred years it was the chief school of Ireland. Ciarán founded it in 544 and died within a year; the house grew into a town of churches, two round towers, a cathedral, and a cemetery in which kings of Connacht and Tara were buried. Its scriptorium produced the Annals of Tigernach and the Chronicon Scotorum, the Lebor na hUidre, and the oldest surviving continuous Irish prose. It was plundered more than forty times by Irish kings, Norsemen and Normans, burned repeatedly, and finally stripped by the English garrison of Athlone in 1552, who carried off even the glass and the bells. The High Cross of the Scriptures still stands. The dictionary records Clonmacnoise for the contrast between the plunder and the text. Forty sackings destroyed the buildings and the treasure, and the writing survived: the word of the Lord endures for ever, which is a claim about the word and not about the monastery that copied it.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines a word as the sign of an idea, and the Scriptures; to endure as to last and continue; to pass away as to cease to be; void as empty and of no effect; and to prosper as to succeed.
webster_full: WORD, n. An articulate sound used as the sign of an idea; in the plural, the Scriptures; the Word of God.
ENDURE, v.i. To last; to continue; to remain; to abide; to brook; to sustain without yielding.
PASS, v.i. To go by, beyond, over or through; to cease to be; to vanish; to go away.
VOID, a. Empty; vacant; not occupied with any visible matter; having no legal or binding force; ineffectual.
PROSPER, v.i. To be successful; to succeed; to make gain or increase; to thrive.
corruption_summary: Shannon monastery and school founded by Ciarán in 544, home of the Irish annals, plundered over forty times and stripped by the Athlone garrison in 1552.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is the one Clonmacnoise proved by surviving as a text rather than as a town: “But the word of the Lord endureth for ever” (1Pe 1:25). Christ puts the same claim in the strongest possible comparison, setting the whole created order on one side and his own sayings on the other: “Heaven and earth shall pass away, but my words shall not pass away” (Mat 24:35).

The live temptation at such a site is antiquarian melancholy, a grief that stops at the ruin and never reaches the thing that outlived it. The annals of the monastery record its forty plunderings; the same scribes copied a word that God himself guarantees will accomplish its errand: “it shall not return unto me void, but it shall accomplish that which I please” (Isa 55:11). The Psalmist states the double ground of confidence, in the word's origin and in its permanence, “Thy word is true from the beginning: and every one of thy righteous judgments endureth for ever” (Psa 119:160). The bells went to Athlone; the sentences did not.

pos: n. (the Wicklow valley monastery founded by Kevin, a see united to Dublin in 1214)
etymology: Irish Gleann Dá Loch, the glen of two lakes, from gleann, a glen, and loch, a lake.
biblical_def: Glendalough is a deep glen in the Wicklow mountains with two lakes in it, where Kevin, or Coemgen, settled as a hermit in the late sixth century and found a community growing round him whether he wanted one or not. The monastery that resulted filled the lower valley with churches, a round tower, a gatehouse and a cathedral, and became a diocese; it was repeatedly burned by Norsemen and by the Irish, and in 1214 the see was united with Dublin, after which the valley declined into a pilgrimage resort with a reputation for riotous gatherings on Kevin's day that the archbishops eventually suppressed. The dictionary records Glendalough for the honest tension in its founder's life, which the hagiographers exaggerated into legend but did not invent: a man goes apart to pray and is given people to teach. Christ commands the closet and the shut door for prayer, and Paul says he wants men free to attend on the Lord without distraction; neither text makes solitude an end, and both assume a man who comes back out.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines a closet as a small private apartment for retirement; secret as hidden and concealed; a distraction as a drawing apart of the mind; to continue as to persevere; and to faint as to lose courage.
webster_full: CLOSET, n. A small room or apartment for retirement; any room for privacy; a private repository of curiosities.
SECRET, a. Separate; hid; concealed from the notice or knowledge of all persons except the individual concerned.
DISTRACTION, n. A drawing apart; separation; a drawing of the mind in different directions; perturbation of mind.
CONTINUE, v.i. To remain in a state, or place; to abide for any time indefinitely; to persevere; to be steadfast.
FAINT, v.i. To lose the animal functions; to lose courage or spirit; to sink into dejection; to grow weak.
corruption_summary: Wicklow valley monastery founded by Kevin, grown from a hermitage into a diocese, united to Dublin in 1214 and later a riotous pilgrimage resort.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is that the shut door is commanded and the shut life is not. Christ gives the command with its reason and its reward: “enter into thy closet, and when thou hast shut thy door, pray to thy Father which is in secret” (Mat 6:6). Paul wants the same freedom from interruption for the single believer, and he says plainly why, “that ye may attend upon the Lord without distraction” (1Co 7:35), which is an aim and not a vocation of hiding.

The two live temptations at Glendalough are both documented in its own history. One is the pilgrimage that turned a hermit's glen into a fair with drink and fighting in it, which the archbishops of Dublin had to put down. The other is to treat withdrawal as the whole of devotion rather than as the room in which devotion is practised. Christ's parable on prayer gives the real discipline, “that men ought always to pray, and not to faint” (Luk 18:1), and Paul puts it as a standing order to ordinary congregations: “Continue in prayer, and watch in the same with thanksgiving” (Col 4:2). Kevin got a community; he kept the hours.

pos: n. (the Meath monastery that became the head of the Columban houses after Iona was sacked, and that gives its name to the Book of Kells)
etymology: Irish Ceanannas Mór, the great head fort or chief residence; the English form comes through Cenannus.
biblical_def: Kells in County Meath was granted to the Columban community in 804 as a refuge after the Norse attacks on Iona, and from the ninth century it was the head house of the familia of Columba. Its round tower, high crosses and the oratory called St Columba's House survive. The Book of Kells, the great illuminated gospel book begun at Iona and probably finished at Kells, was kept there for seven hundred years until it was taken to Dublin in the seventeenth century; a note in the Annals records its theft from the sacristy in 1007 and its recovery from under a sod, stripped of its gold cover. A reforming synod met at Kells in 1152 and gave Ireland its four archbishoprics and the pallium. The dictionary records Kells for the gospel book. Men who had been burned out of Iona spent their exile covering four gospels with gold and interlace, and the labour makes sense only on the premise that the text is what it claims: a word like fire and a hammer, quick and powerful, which opened the disciples' hearts on the Emmaus road.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines illumination as the act of adorning with colors and gold; a hammer as an instrument for driving and breaking; quick as living and active; to pierce as to penetrate; and a discerner as one who distinguishes.
webster_full: ILLUMINATION, n. The act of illuminating or rendering luminous; the adorning of books and manuscripts with colored and ornamented letters.
HAMMER, n. An instrument for driving nails, beating metals, and the like; any instrument of force applied by blows.
QUICK, a. Living; alive; not dead; speedy; hasty; done in little time; active; brisk.
PIERCE, v.t. To thrust into with a pointed instrument; to penetrate; to enter; to force a way into.
DISCERNER, n. One who discerns, distinguishes or perceives; that which distinguishes.
corruption_summary: Meath monastery that became the head of the Columban houses after the Norse sack of Iona, keeper of the Book of Kells, and site of the reforming synod of 1152.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is the premise behind every labour spent on a manuscript, which is what the text is. The LORD asks it as a question with two images in it: “Is not my word like as a fire? saith the LORD; and like a hammer that breaketh the rock in pieces?” (Jer 23:29). The writer to the Hebrews describes the same operation in a man rather than on a rock, “For the word of God is quick, and powerful, and sharper than any twoedged sword” (Heb 4:12).

The live temptation with a famous illuminated book is to admire the vellum and ignore the sentences, which is a reversal of everything the scribes intended. The disciples on the Emmaus road give the right account of what happens when the text is opened: “Did not our heart burn within us, while he talked with us by the way, and while he opened to us the scriptures?” (Luk 24:32). Isaiah tells a people to look back to their origin without worshipping it, “look unto the rock whence ye are hewn” (Isa 51:1), which is exactly the right use of a monastery's inheritance and the wrong use of a display case.

pos: n. (the Offaly monastery founded by Columba, home of the Book of Durrow, the oldest surviving complete insular gospel book)
etymology: Irish Darmhagh, the plain of the oaks, from dair, an oak, and magh, a plain.
biblical_def: Durrow in County Offaly was founded by Columba about 553, before he left for Iona, and was the chief of his Irish houses; Adomnán calls it the monastery of the oak plain. Its high cross and the stump of its round tower stand in a graveyard beside a small church. Its treasure is the Book of Durrow, a gospel book of the second half of the seventh century, the oldest surviving fully decorated insular gospel book and the direct ancestor of the Lindisfarne Gospels and the Book of Kells; it was kept at Durrow in a shrine made for it by an Irish king, was used into the seventeenth century for dipping in water to cure sick cattle, and is now in Dublin. The dictionary records Durrow for the plain commission the book contains. Four gospels, decorated for four or five years of a man's life, carry a command addressed to every creature and every nation, and the labour of copying is only intelligible as obedience to that command: go, preach, teach, and the sending is the condition of the preaching.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines a gospel as God's word and the history of Christ; to preach as to proclaim the gospel; a creature as a created being; to baptize as to administer the rite of baptism; and to send as to dispatch on an errand.
webster_full: GOSPEL, n. The history of the birth, life, actions, death, resurrection, ascension and doctrine of Jesus Christ; God's word; the whole scheme of salvation.
PREACH, v.i. To pronounce a public discourse on a religious subject; to proclaim the gospel; to discourse on the gospel way of salvation.
CREATURE, n. That which is created; every being besides the Creator, or every thing not self-existent.
BAPTIZE, v.t. To administer the sacrament of baptism to; to christen.
SEND, v.t. To cause to go or pass from one place to another; to dispatch on a message, an errand or a commission.
corruption_summary: Columba's chief Irish house in Offaly, founded about 553, home of the Book of Durrow, the oldest complete insular gospel book.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is the commission that a gospel book exists to carry. Mark states it with no limits of race or place: “Go ye into all the world, and preach the gospel to every creature” (Mar 16:15). Matthew adds the nations, the sign and the teaching, “Go ye therefore, and teach all nations, baptizing them in the name of the Father, and of the Son, and of the Holy Ghost” (Mat 28:19).

The live temptation is the one Durrow's own book suffered, a text treated as a charm. For a century or more the book was dipped in water that was then given to sick cattle, which is superstition working on the very pages that command preaching. The command itself includes the whole duty, “Teaching them to observe all things whatsoever I have commanded you” (Mat 28:20), and Paul fixes the order by which it is carried out, which is sending and then speaking: “And how shall they preach, except they be sent?” (Rom 10:15). The cure for a relic is a sermon.

Go ye therefore, and teach all nations, baptizing them in the name of the Father, and of the Son, and of the Holy Ghost:
Teaching them to observe all things whatsoever I have commanded you: and, lo, I am with you alway, even unto the end of the world. Amen.
And how shall they preach, except they be sent? as it is written, How beautiful are the feet of them that preach the gospel of peace, and bring glad tidings of good things!

pos: n. (the Galway see founded about 557 by Brendan the Navigator, with a famous Romanesque west doorway)
etymology: Irish Cluain Fearta, the meadow of the grave or of the miracle, from cluain, a meadow, and feart, a grave.
biblical_def: Clonfert in east Galway was founded about 557 by Brendan, who is buried there, and was a monastery, a school and then a diocese confirmed at Rathbreasail. Its cathedral keeps the most elaborate Romanesque doorway in Ireland, a gable of carved heads and chevrons from about 1180. Brendan himself is known chiefly from the Navigatio Sancti Brendani, a Latin voyage tale written three or four centuries after his death, in which he and his monks sail west for seven years, keep Easter on the back of a whale, and find the Land of Promise of the Saints; the book was one of the most widely copied works of the Middle Ages. Behind the legend there is a real and verifiable practice, the peregrinatio, by which Irish monks put to sea with no destination for the love of God, and reached the Hebrides, Orkney, the Faroes and Iceland. The dictionary records Clonfert for the sober fact inside the tale. The Psalter had already described these men before they sailed: those who go down to the sea in ships see the works of the LORD and his wonders in the deep.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines a ship as a vessel of large size for navigation; the deep as the sea; an island as land surrounded by water; to escape as to flee from danger; and to renew as to make new again.
webster_full: SHIP, n. In a general sense, a vessel or building of a peculiar structure, adapted to navigation; in strictness, a vessel with three masts.
DEEP, n. The sea; the abyss of waters; the ocean; any abyss or unfathomable gulf.
ISLAND, n. A tract of land surrounded by water; a body of land encompassed by the sea, a lake or a river.
ESCAPE, v.i. To flee from and avoid; to get out of the way; to be free or safe from danger.
RENEW, v.t. To renovate; to restore to a former state, or to a good state, after decay or depravation; to make new again.
corruption_summary: East Galway see founded about 557 by Brendan the Navigator, with Ireland's finest Romanesque doorway and the voyage legend that made it famous.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is the one the voyage legend decorates and the Psalter states soberly, that the sea is a school for men who have to trust God in it. Of such men it is written, “They that go down to the sea in ships, that do business in great waters” (Psa 107:23), and the consequence is not adventure but sight: “These see the works of the LORD, and his wonders in the deep” (Psa 107:24).

The live temptation is to let a tall tale stand in for the real obedience underneath it. Irish monks did put to sea without a destination, and the islands they reached were real; the whale and the Land of Promise were not. Isaiah summons the islands to a hearing rather than to a legend: “Keep silence before me, O islands; and let the people renew their strength” (Isa 41:1). Luke's way of reporting a shipwreck is the right model for a voyage narrative, which is to name the place and move on: “then they knew that the island was called Melita” (Act 28:1).

pos: n. (the Kerry see of Brendan, the most westerly diocese of Ireland, facing the Atlantic)
etymology: Irish Ard Fhearta, the height of the grave, from ard, a height, and feart, a grave or miracle.
biblical_def: Ardfert lies in north Kerry a few miles from the Atlantic, the see of a diocese that Brendan is said to have founded before he went to Clonfert, and the most westerly in Ireland. The ruined cathedral of St Brendan, begun in the twelfth century and enlarged in the thirteenth, stands with two smaller churches and a Franciscan friary nearby. The diocese was poor, Gaelic-speaking and remote, and at the Reformation it was among the places where the new establishment had almost no foothold; the cathedral was wrecked in 1641 and never restored. The dictionary records Ardfert for its geography. From the hill at Ardfert the next land westwards is America, and the Irish church that sent men out from such places had taken the terms of the commission literally: witnesses unto the uttermost part of the earth. Scripture speaks of the isles waiting, the ships of Tarshish bringing sons from far, and feet beautiful upon the mountains because they bring good tidings, and the men who sailed from the Kerry coast had read all three.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines a witness as one who gives testimony; the uttermost as the furthest extent; tidings as news; to publish as to make known; and an inheritance as an estate received by descent.
webster_full: WITNESS, n. Testimony; attestation of a fact or event; one who sees or hears a thing and can give an account of it.
UTTERMOST, a. Extreme; being in the furthest, greatest or highest degree; the furthest part or extent.
TIDINGS, n. News; advice; information; intelligence; account of what has taken place.
PUBLISH, v.t. To discover to mankind; to make known to a people something before unknown or kept secret; to proclaim.
INHERITANCE, n. An estate derived from an ancestor to an heir by succession; a possession received by gift or divine appointment.
corruption_summary: The most westerly Irish see, Brendan's Kerry foundation, poor and Gaelic-speaking, its cathedral wrecked in 1641 and never restored.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is the geographical reach of the commission, which the Irish west took at face value. Christ names the limit in a way that has no limit: his witnesses are to go “both in Jerusalem, and in all Judaea, and in Samaria, and unto the uttermost part of the earth” (Act 1:8). Isaiah had promised traffic in the other direction too, “Surely the isles shall wait for me, and the ships of Tarshish first” (Isa 60:9).

The live temptation at the edge of the map is to think of oneself as the edge of the work, a church too remote and too poor to be a sending church. Ardfert was both and sent men anyway. Isaiah praises the messengers themselves, feet that are beautiful because of what they carry: “How beautiful upon the mountains are the feet of him that bringeth good tidings” (Isa 52:7). And the scope promised to the Son is not partial, “Ask of me, and I shall give thee the heathen for thine inheritance, and the uttermost parts of the earth for thy possession” (Psa 2:8), which includes the Atlantic coast and everything beyond it.

Surely the isles shall wait for me, and the ships of Tarshish first, to bring thy sons from far, their silver and their gold with them, unto the name of the LORD thy God, and to the Holy One of Israel, because he hath glorified thee.

pos: n. (the ancient Munster primatial see of Ailbe, absorbed into Cashel in 1568)
etymology: Irish Imleach Iubhair, the lakeside or borderland of the yew, from imleach, a marshy edge.
biblical_def: Emly in west Tipperary was the chief church of Munster before Cashel, the see of Ailbe, whom the Munster tradition sets beside Patrick and sometimes before him, and whose rule survives in Irish verse. Its bishops claimed the primacy of the province into the twelfth century, and the synod of Rathbreasail in 1111 made Emly one of the twelve Munster sees while giving the archbishopric to Cashel. From then on it declined, and in 1568 it was formally united to Cashel, under whose archbishops the title survives to this day; the old cathedral is gone entirely and a parish church stands on the mound. The dictionary records Emly for the disappearance. A see with the oldest claim in the province was swallowed by a younger neighbour and the name was kept as a courtesy. That is painful to a diocese and harmless to the church, because the unity Scripture asserts is not a unity of jurisdictions but of one body with one Lord, one faith and one baptism, in which the members are members of one another whatever the map says.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines a body as the material organized frame, and a collective whole; one as single in number and undivided; faith as belief and assent of the mind; a member as a part of a body; and unity as the state of being one.
webster_full: BODY, n. The frame of an animal; the material substance of an animal; a collective mass; a number of individuals united.
ONE, a. Single in number; individual; not two or more; the same; undivided.
FAITH, n. Belief; the assent of the mind to the truth of what is declared by another, resting on his authority and veracity.
MEMBER, n. A limb of animal bodies; a part of a body or whole; a subordinate part of a main body.
UNITY, n. The state of being one; oneness; concord; conjunction; agreement; uniformity.
corruption_summary: Ancient primatial see of Munster, the church of Ailbe, which lost the archbishopric to Cashel in 1111 and was absorbed by it in 1568.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is the kind of unity the New Testament actually asserts, which is not administrative. Paul lists it as a set of facts rather than as a programme: “There is one body, and one Spirit, even as ye are called in one hope of your calling” (Eph 4:4), and the list continues with the three things no amalgamation can create or destroy, “One Lord, one faith, one baptism” (Eph 4:5).

The live temptation when a jurisdiction is lost is to grieve as though the church had been diminished, or else to argue precedence between sees that are both the Lord's. Paul's figure forbids both: “For as the body is one, and hath many members, and all the members of that one body, being many, are one body: so also is Christ” (1Co 12:12). Membership is mutual and not hierarchical, “So we, being many, are one body in Christ, and every one members one of another” (Rom 12:5). Emly kept its people and lost its primacy, and only one of those losses would have mattered.

pos: n. (the Meath monastery of Finnian, called the teacher of the saints of Ireland, whose pupils are reckoned the twelve apostles of Ireland)
etymology: Irish Cluain Ioraird, the meadow of Iorard, from cluain, a water meadow.
biblical_def: Clonard on the Boyne in County Meath was founded about 520 by Finnian, who had studied in Wales, and it became the school from which the second generation of the Irish church came. The tradition names twelve of his pupils as the twelve apostles of Ireland, and the list includes Ciarán of Clonmacnoise, Columba of Iona, Brendan of Clonfert, Kevin of Glendalough and Columbanus's teacher Comgall; whatever the exact number, the founders of nearly every great Irish house of the sixth century were taught at Clonard, and the chroniclers call Finnian the teacher of the saints of Ireland. The monastery itself was burned and plundered many times and is now a field with a font in the parish church. The dictionary records Clonard for the one thing a teacher can leave behind. Finnian wrote no surviving book and built nothing that stands, and the whole Irish church of the following century came out of his classroom. Scripture frames the duty exactly so: ask the former age, remember what the fathers taught, hold what has been handed down, and declare it to the generation following.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines a tradition as doctrine delivered from father to son; to enquire as to ask and seek information; a landmark as a mark to designate a boundary; to declare as to make known; and an age as a period of time or generation.
webster_full: TRADITION, n. The delivery of opinions, doctrines, practices, rites and customs from father to son, or from ancestors to posterity; oral delivery.
ENQUIRE, v.i. To ask a question; to seek for truth or information by asking questions; to search or examine into.
LANDMARK, n. Any mark or fixed object, as a marked tree, a stone, a ditch, by which the limits of a farm or estate are known.
DECLARE, v.t. To make known; to tell explicitly; to manifest or communicate plainly to others by words.
AGE, n. A particular period of time, as distinguished from others; a generation of men; the people who live at a particular period.
corruption_summary: Meath monastery founded about 520 by Finnian, the teacher of the saints of Ireland, whose pupils founded nearly every great Irish house of that century.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is that teaching is the one inheritance the church is commanded to pass on. The Psalter makes the handing on itself an act of praise: “One generation shall praise thy works to another, and shall declare thy mighty acts” (Psa 145:4). Job's friend, however badly he applies it, states the right instinct toward what came before: “For enquire, I pray thee, of the former age, and prepare thyself to the search of their fathers” (Job 8:8).

The live temptation is a false choice between Scripture and the things handed down in the church. Paul uses the word himself and tells the Thessalonians to keep what they were taught by two means: “stand fast, and hold the traditions which ye have been taught, whether by word, or our epistle” (2Th 2:15) — apostolic teaching, written and spoken, and nothing beyond it. Solomon's warning about boundaries is the right picture of how such an inheritance is treated: “Remove not the ancient landmark, which thy fathers have set” (Pro 22:28). Finnian set landmarks, and twelve men carried them across Ireland.

pos: n. (the island off the Llyn peninsula, called the island of twenty thousand saints, where three pilgrimages were reckoned equal to one to Rome)
etymology: Norse Barðr's ey, Bard's island; the Welsh is Ynys Enlli, the island of the tides or of the current.
biblical_def: Bardsey lies two miles off the tip of the Llyn peninsula across a race of tide that can keep a boat ashore for weeks. A monastery was founded there in the sixth century, traditionally by Cadfan, and the island became the chief burial place of the Welsh church; the medieval claim was that twenty thousand saints lay in its soil, and the papacy is said to have allowed that three pilgrimages to Bardsey counted as one to Rome. The Augustinian abbey of St Mary was dissolved in 1537 and the island passed to lay owners; it is now a bird observatory with a small chapel. The dictionary records Bardsey for the arithmetic of indulgence, three voyages to a Welsh island discharging the debt of a journey to Italy, which is a transaction of a kind Scripture nowhere recognises. What it does recognise is that generations pass and the earth remains, that the creation itself will wear out like a garment while God remains, and that a believer's portion is a heritage received and not a credit earned.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines a generation as a single succession of men; to abide as to remain and continue; a vesture as a garment; a heritage as an inheritance; and goodly as pleasant and excellent.
webster_full: GENERATION, n. A single succession in natural descent; the people of the same period; production; formation.
ABIDE, v.i. To rest, or dwell; to tarry or stay for a short time; to continue permanently or in the same state.
VESTURE, n. A garment; a robe; a covering; dress; habit; clothing.
HERITAGE, n. Inheritance; an estate that passes from an ancestor to an heir by descent; the people of God, as his possession.
GOODLY, a. Being of a handsome form; beautiful; graceful; pleasant; agreeable; excellent.
corruption_summary: Island off the Llyn peninsula, chief burial place of the Welsh church and a pilgrimage resort where three voyages were reckoned equal to one journey to Rome.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is the right way to think about an island full of graves, and Scripture is calm about it: “One generation passeth away, and another generation cometh: but the earth abideth for ever” (Ecc 1:4). Even the earth's permanence is relative, for the Psalmist sets the creation itself against its Maker: “as a vesture shalt thou change them, and they shall be changed” (Psa 102:26).

The live temptation at Bardsey was arithmetic, three crossings to the island discharging the merit of a pilgrimage to Rome, and the pricing of grace is the error whether the currency is voyages, money or years. The writer to the Hebrews applies the Psalm directly to Christ and leaves nothing for a transaction to buy: “They shall perish; but thou remainest; and they all shall wax old as doth a garment” (Heb 1:11). What the believer actually holds is a portion assigned to him, received and not reckoned up: “The lines are fallen unto me in pleasant places; yea, I have a goodly heritage” (Psa 16:6). Twenty thousand graves on an island do not add to it.

pos: n. (the Down monastery of Finnian, whose copied psalter provoked the quarrel that sent Columba to Iona)
etymology: Irish Magh Bhile, the plain of the sacred tree, from magh, a plain, and bile, an ancient tree.
biblical_def: Moville on Strangford Lough in County Down was founded about 540 by Finnian, called Finnian of Moville to distinguish him from Finnian of Clonard, a man who had studied at Whithorn and who is said to have brought a copy of the Latin Gospels back from Rome. The story attached to that book is the most famous quarrel in Irish church history: Columba copied it without permission, Finnian claimed the copy, the high king Diarmait judged for Finnian, and the dispute fed into the battle of Cúl Dreimhne in 561 in which thousands died. Columba was arraigned before a synod, and whether as sentence or as self-imposed penance he left Ireland for Iona, undertaking to win more souls than had fallen in the battle. The copy, called the Cathach, survives as the oldest Irish manuscript. The dictionary records Moville for what the episode cost and for how it ended. The sacrifices God accepts are named plainly as a broken spirit and a contrite heart, and the one place he promises to dwell besides the high and holy place is with the man who has them.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines contrite as broken-hearted for sin; a sacrifice as an offering made to God; humble as having a low opinion of oneself; to revive as to restore life or vigor; and justly as according to right.
webster_full: CONTRITE, a. Literally, worn or bruised; hence, broken-hearted for sin; deeply affected with grief and sorrow for having offended God.
SACRIFICE, n. An offering made to God; any thing consecrated and offered to God; destruction or surrender of any thing for the sake of something else.
HUMBLE, a. Low; opposed to high or lofty; modest; meek; submissive; having a low opinion of one's self.
REVIVE, v.t. To bring again to life; to reanimate; to raise from languor or depression; to recover.
JUSTLY, adv. In a just manner; equitably; according to right; honestly; properly.
corruption_summary: Down monastery of Finnian of Moville, whose psalter Columba copied without leave, provoking the judgment and the battle that sent Columba to Iona.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is the end of the story rather than the quarrel in it. Whatever the rights of the copied book, what came out of Cúl Dreimhne was a man undone by his own share in the slaughter, and the offering such a man can make is named exactly: “The sacrifices of God are a broken spirit: a broken and a contrite heart, O God, thou wilt not despise” (Psa 51:17). Isaiah adds the astonishing promise attached to that condition, that the high and lofty One dwells “with him also that is of a contrite and humble spirit” (Isa 57:15).

The live temptation is to let a dispute over property, even church property, become a war, and the Irish church did exactly that over a psalter. Micah had already reduced the whole requirement to three clauses that would have prevented it: what the LORD requires is “to do justly, and to love mercy, and to walk humbly with thy God” (Mic 6:8). And Christ's prayer makes the unity of his people a matter of the world's belief, “That they all may be one; as thou, Father, art in me, and I in thee” (Joh 17:21). Two abbots at law over a book is the opposite of that witness; Iona was the restitution.
